title: An alien audits your robot vacuum
answer: Humans built a disc to clean the floor. Then they gave it a name. In a study of 30 owners, 21 had named their robot vacuum, 16 called it "he", and one introduced it to his parents.

notes.text: Sung, Guo, Grinter & Christensen (2007), "My Roomba Is Rambo": Intimate Home Appliances, UbiComp 2007 (Georgia Tech).

pin: What is your robot vacuum called?
transcript: Field report four. Subject: humans.
They built a machine to clean the floor.
It is a disc. It has no face.
Researchers visited thirty owners.
Twenty-one had given it a name.
Sixteen called it "he".
Some clean first. So it has less work.
One introduced it to his parents.
Verdict:
Adorable. They have named me too.
What is yours called?

checked.claim: Of 30 robot vacuum owners studied, 21 had named it and 16 called it "he"

title: An alien studies how humans hunt
answer: Humans are slow, but they can keep moving in heat that stops faster animals. Hunters in the Kalahari were recorded running down kudu over 2 to 5 hours and 25 to 35 km, at about 40°C.

notes.text: Liebenberg (2006), "Persistence Hunting by Modern Hunter-Gatherers", Current Anthropology 47(6).

pin: How far could you run before you had to stop?
transcript: Field report five. Subject: humans.
They are slower than their prey.
So they do not sprint. They keep coming.
Recorded in the Kalahari. At forty degrees.
Two to five hours. Thirty-five kilometres.
The prey overheats. It has to stop.
The human does not. It leaks to stay cool.
Then it walks up to its dinner.
Verdict:
Terrifying. Do not run.
How far could you go?

checked.claim: Recorded persistence hunts lasted about 2 to 5 hours over 25 to 35 km at 40 to 42°C
checked.verdict: Confirmed, from a small number of recorded hunts

title: An alien tries to understand spicy food
answer: Chillies burn mammals but not birds, which spread their seeds. Humans grow them on purpose. Psychologist Paul Rozin calls the pleasure "benign masochism", and estimates that about a third of people eat hot peppers every day.

notes.text: Rozin & Schiller (1980), "The nature and acquisition of a preference for chili pepper by humans", Motivation and Emotion 4: 77–101.

pin: How hot can you go? Name your pepper.
transcript: Field report six. Subject: humans.
A plant makes a chemical that burns mammals.
It is a warning. Do not eat me.
Birds cannot feel it. Mammals stay away.
Humans farm it.
A third of them eat it every day.
They sweat. They cry. They ask for more.
Their scientists call it benign masochism.
Verdict:
Absurd. Pass the sauce.
How hot can you go?

checked.claim: Rozin calls the liking of chilli burn "benign masochism"; well over 2 billion adults enjoy it

title: An alien visits a haunted house
answer: Fear tells an animal to leave. Humans buy tickets to it. In a haunted house in Denmark, 110 visitors wore heart-rate monitors: they enjoyed it most at a middle level of fear, and less when it was too mild or too strong.

notes.text: Andersen et al. (2020), "Playing With Fear: A Field Study in Recreational Horror", Psychological Science 31(12): 1497–1510.

pin: What scared you just the right amount?
transcript: Field report seven. Subject: humans.
Fear is their alarm. It means: leave.
Humans buy tickets to it.
Dark houses. Actors dressed as zombies.
Researchers wired 110 visitors to heart monitors.
Too little fear: bored.
Too much: miserable.
In the middle: delighted.
Verdict:
Reckless. I have bought a ticket.
What scared you just enough?

checked.claim: 110 haunted-house visitors (ages 12 to 57) enjoyed it most at a middle level of fear

title: Could you outrun a T. rex?
answer: Yup says easy. Nope has numbers: a 2017 computer model found that T. rex could not run without breaking its legs, but its fast walk still reached about 19 km/h (12 mph). You decide.

notes.text: Sellers et al. (2017), "Investigating the running abilities of Tyrannosaurus rex using stress-constrained multibody dynamic analysis", PeerJ 5: e3420.
The paper limits T. rex to walking. The figure of about 19 km/h (12 mph) is as reported from the study; the paper itself gives no single top speed for that walk.

pin: Run, hide or stand still? Vote.
transcript: Yup: Could you outrun a T. rex? Easy!
Nope: Good news. It could not run.
Yup: Ha! Told you!
Nope: Its bones would have snapped. A 2017 study.
Yup: So I just jog away!
Nope: Its fastest walk: about nineteen kilometres an hour.
Yup: …That is faster than I jog.
Nope: That is a five-minute mile. Good luck.
Yup: So could you outrun it?

checked.claim: A 2017 computer model found running would overload the leg bones of T. rex, limiting it to walking

title: Hot day: hot drink or cold drink?
answer: Nine men cycled for 75 minutes while drinking water between 1.5°C and 50°C. With the hot water their bodies stored less heat: they sweated more, and the sweat evaporated. It only works where sweat can dry, and the lead researcher says the effect is small.

notes.text: Bain, Lesperance & Jay (2012), "Body heat storage during physical activity is lower with hot fluid ingestion under conditions that permit full evaporation", Acta Physiologica 206(2): 98–108.

pin: Hot tea or iced water on a hot day? Vote.
transcript: Yup: Hot day! Ice water! Obviously!
Nope: A hot drink can cool you more.
Yup: That is nonsense.
Nope: Nine cyclists. Ottawa. Hot water won.
Yup: How?!
Nope: Hot drink, more sweat. Sweat dries, you cool.
Yup: So I drink tea in a heatwave!
Nope: Only if your sweat can dry. Humid? You lose.
Yup: Hot or cold? Your pick.

checked.claim: With 50°C water, cyclists stored less body heat than with 1.5°C, 10°C or 37°C water, when sweat could fully evaporate

title: The knot that unties itself (it is geometry)
answer: A knotted loop cannot be undone in our three dimensions. With a fourth direction to move in, one strand can step past another without touching it, so every knot comes apart.

notes.text: Standard knot theory: Livingston, "Knot Theory" (Mathematical Association of America, 1993), chapter 9.

transcript: Tie a knot. Join the ends.
Now it can never come undone.
Pull. Twist. Still stuck.
Unless you ask me.
I nudge one strand in my direction.
It steps past the other. Without touching.
Every knot does this. Every single one.
Mathematicians proved it.
In my world, you could not tie your shoes.
I wear slippers.

checked.claim: Every knotted loop can be undone in four dimensions

title: 23 million people share your birthday
answer: About 8.3 billion people share 365 days, so roughly 23 million people have your birthday. For 29 February it is about 6 million.

notes.text: United Nations, World Population Prospects 2024, divided by the days in a year.
These are averages: real birthdays are not spread perfectly evenly.

pin: When is your birthday? Find your 23 million.
transcript: I'm Murmur. One dot, a million people.
Think of your birthday.
Now watch. I'll sort myself by day.
Twelve months. Every day of the year.
These dots share your day.
Twenty-three of them. Twenty-three million people.
All one year older on the same day.
Born on the twenty-ninth of February?
You are rarer. About six dots.
Which day is yours?

checked.claim: 8.3 billion ÷ 365.25 days ≈ 22.7 million people per birthday; ÷ 1,461 ≈ 5.7 million for 29 February
